And, thanks to Ms. Barnes, caseworkers did not have to waste their time interrogating this family; leaving them more time to find children in real danger.

comments.body: As a South African, I’m looking forward to reading this book, if for no other reason than to see how the views of my countrymen and women are represented. We were in the very darkest days of the rebellion against apartheid in 1986. Foreigners and local ideologues reacted with horror at Simon’s violation of a cultural boycott they had imposed without really consulting ordinary people in the country. And yet everywhere in SA, the album’s tracks were playing in bars, shebeens, beaches, braaivleis, and the cassette decks of our old skorokoros (beat up cars). We saw it as a welcome reflection of our culture’s inherent vibrancy and essential positivity, even in the face of apartheid terror. To this day, many South Africans of all colours regard Graceland as part of “the soundtrack to liberation.” Questioning its appropriateness apparently still happens elsewhere; but not here in South Africa, where the music was made.

She has taken aim at what she clearly believes to be a failure or weakness, the "no contact" approach, and she's not entirely wrong in saying that our tendency is to give up too easily, to look for permission to quit the effort. Again, she leaves out an important part, that some people do the hard work, they don't give up, and end up living a life marred by unresolvable pain.

All to say, there's merit in both approaches, doing the hard work of bringing a relationship to a point of fulfillment, but also doing the hard work of recognizing when no amount of effort is going to achieve that fulfillment. Subscribing to an ethic that says loving and being loved by another is an absolute mandate to "honor that blessing" denies the reality that for some people, that "love" can be destructive.

I would never get up and out on my own motivation, but I do love being out on the beach with the early birds— whether human, dogs or actual birds. 
I met a young friend who showed me pictures she has taken of an amazing amount of wildlife she observes right here in the margins of the suburbs— she has already 200 birds on her life list without going far afield. Also, mink, turtles, and frogs. So heartening to see. It made me think about camouflage and keeping secret worlds hidden. It also made me think how these magical worlds are not far away— we just need to be able to pay attention and be patient. It’s the same with people— we cover our vulnerability with fashion, art and humor— while our eyes meet others— I love everything about you!  This world seems to be here so we can marvel at its variety. I can report that the ducks were in a row on the seawall. The bunny did not interrupt its breakfast of dewy grass as we passed. Hi, neighbors! Time for a second cup of coffee. Life is tough. The news is disturbing. Yet love is there— the chipmunk looks like an oak leaf. The ducks splash into the still dawn water. I want to add two things: give preference to the classics, the true and tried repositories of human wisdom, the beautifully written texts some of us have treasured through the centuries. The second things I want to say is more complicated: you see, reading is a sequential experience, beginning from the left at the top of the page, and descending to the bottom. To learn to read is to submit the wholistic experiencing of the world a child confronts and enjoys, to a sequential system which will from then on control the child's experiences. Some children --myself included -- recoil before this sequencing imposition, and this is one reason why reading has declined today. Many children don't want their world to change, their experiencing of their world, so they prefer the more holistic experience of the cell phone and the conversation with their peers. In the old times, illustrations served the purpose of recovering the whole while the sequencing was taking place. Illustrations seemed to say, "Don't worry, go on and sequence, you can always recover the whole in a picture." We need to provide today something akin to the recovery of wholeness we give up by sequencing and reading. I don't know how this can be done, but I feel strongly that herein lies a secret: living is BOTH sequential and wholistic, bound by the passage of time and by the momentary wholeness of vision. If people are truly serious about gaining insight and education from reading, even with audiobooks, I'm not really too against it, but I NEVER see anyone even listening to ANY audiobooks, educational or otherwise.

I've only seen people showing off fictional audio novels.

Like I said, I guess if that's their preference...

Personally, I don't t like to do audiobooks because they're SO MUCH more slow.

Listening to someone speak the words takes much longer (for me) than reading them.  I can finish reading a novel in a few days.  It would take weeks to listen to it...

comments.body: My extensive 40+ years in education has notice the ups and Sowa’s in literacy rates in our schools. Teachers are working tirelessly in helping to make corrections in our literacy approaches.many of these approaches are not new, but are appearing to have successes. The caveat is this. Parents have to form reading groups within their family groups!! Kids need to see their homes with books and their parents valuing reading. They need to have a book placed into their hands, not devices. Yes, it’s a bit more work and the interactions are time consuming but without it literacy is indeed doomed.

comments.name: Julie
comments.body:
A six month lead is incredibly optimistic. The Cold War analogy seems apt, but the weapon is different. Invisible and can travel through any internet connection. The chips are not the hard to acquire especially in a country that manufactures electronics. 

Nobody has to figure anything out or get their hands on highly enriched uranium here. China and any of the country that wants to can simply train their models on the output of other models at this point and get pretty close, and it’s hard to imagine there aren’t plenty of tech bros in China as well who are perfectly capable of giving it some extra nudges.

The question isn’t that though. What other countries are just as close? Why would we assume it’s going to be another two-sided battle between the largest countries? Soon pretty much anyone will be able to manage this. Cutting edge AI designed for harming each other will accelerate and we will all be worse off for it.

Thankfully we also have plenty of people who remember not that long ago when we didn’t connect critical infrastructure to the entire digital world. The sooner we accept that a couple of months edge in AI acceleratism is basically meaningless in the long term, the sooner we disconnect things that matter instead of just hoping we can advance security just as fast, the better off we’ll be.

It’s not a matter of who can advance the AI the best, it’s a matter of who can protect themselves from AI the best.

comments.name: Susannah
comments.body: AI has yet to prove its worth in industry, yet companies are rushing to buy it and fire, or at least don't hire, employees.  If AI is truly the equivalent of "digital nuclear weapons," then we should put efforts and money into digital defense.  Above all, we should have competent, knowledgeable people in charge.  I wouldn't count on anything that will be to our benefit when Trump and Xi meet.

comments.name: David E. Sanger
comments.body: AI is touching all aspects of life - at home, in the classroom, on the job market. It has triggered fears of mass unemployment, predictions of huge productivity gains and shown new ways to diagnose disease early. But no place is AI- -driven change coming faster than in national security. So we gathered four reporters who cover the White House, cyber, intelligence and trade for a broad look at the challenges and chaos in recent policymaking - the first of many such deep dives, I hope.

comments.name: PJ
comments.body:
AI dominance - but don’t build the data centers. 

AI dominance - but restrict how the Defense Department can use it. 

AI dominance - but don’t displace jobs. 

AI dominance - but sue the American companies developing it. 

AI dominance - but fight the energy infrastructure needed to power it. 

Meanwhile, China faces none of these political, legal and regulatory constraints. Once Beijing decides something is a national priority, it can execute.

The US is an open democracy. As technological change accelerates, the gap between how fast we need to make consequential decisions and how fast our political, legal and regulatory systems will let them, is only going to grow. 

AI may be the first place where that mismatch becomes a serious strategic disadvantage.

We say AI dominance is a national-security imperative, but seem unwilling to accept many of the tradeoffs required to achieve it.

comments.name: Nogi Ichida
comments.body:
Not to predict any nation's fate, but historically, when an empire is in decline, people naturally assume it should preserve what it has and get rid of burdens that are no longer necessary to maintain. Yet history often shows the opposite: declining empires tend to double down, sometimes on steroids, trying to stop what may ultimately be unstoppable.

I don't understand why the U.S. is so obsessed with AI, as if it were a magic wand that could reverse everything. So much money and resources are being thrown at this magic wand, while a seemingly inflated stock market makes a very small number of people extremely wealthy. Meanwhile, long-overdue problems such as infrastructure, education, and health care continue to receive far less attention. Let alone the current quagmire with Iran is adding gas to the flame. 

China is not alone in this AI obsession. Its AI industry is also growing on steroids, but with somewhat more self-control. Because of the higher purchasing power of the RMB domestically, Chinese companies don't necessarily have to spend the same extreme amounts of cash to achieve similar levels of deployment.

China, however, faces its own serious problems: deflationary pressure and stagnant wages remain major challenges, and I don't think the government  there has given them enough attention.

articles.title: The U.S. Military Wants A.I. Dominance. Feuds and China May Thwart It.

articles.summary: The administration is veering wildly in its response to the national security implications of A.I. as China, America’s main technological and military rival, charges ahead.

comments.name: Nonna
comments.body: His parishioners are very lucky to have such a dedicated priest. What a beautiful example of how religion is supposed to bring people together, not separate. Despite feeling like an outsider at times, he is bringing something invaluable to these communities. I hope he gets the help that he needs and that he can thrive along with the people he serves.

comments.name: Motoko Rich
comments.body:
When I moved to Rome, a Ghanian priest I met in an Italian class pointed out a quiet shift: with fewer Italian-born men entering the priesthood, African pastors were increasingly stepping in to shepherd parishes across the country, not just study theology or canon law.

Curious about their day-to-day reality, we shadowed Rev. Vincent Souly over a weekend. He opened his life to us — from presiding over Masses and making home visits to reflecting on the burden of serving a community where his heritage can complicate his welcome.

comments.name: PWD
comments.body: This is a lovely story. There is a priest shortage, and even 30 years ago in metro-NYC, we had priests from other nations. Father Souly is highly educated, and with his appointment as diocesan head canonical law officer, he will no doubt be staying there for a long time.  I am happy for him and for the parishioners of the church circuit he caretakes.

comments.name: Susan
comments.body: Thank you for this uplifting article.  With daily news filled with reports of calamitous disasters, violence, and corruption, it is wonderful to be reminded that there are good and selfless people in this world who recognize and are willing to respond to the needs of others.  With a doctoral degree from a Pontifical university, Father Souly could very well have pursued a distinguished career in Church hierarchy. The fact that he chose a very unglamorous life as a rural priest says something powerful about his giving character. The Italians are blessed to have him as their priest.

articles.title: With Priests Scarce in Rural Italy, an African Pastor Is Filling the Void
articles.byline: Motoko Rich, Josephine de La Bruyère and Alessandro Grassani
articles.summary: Immigrants have long eased labor shortages on farms and factories in Italy. But churches also need foreign-born priests, like the Rev. Vincent Souly of the Ivory Coast.
